title: AI in Space: Helpful Assistant or Sci-Fi Villain?
summary: In movies like WALL-E, AI runs entire spaceships. In real life, AI is helping explore space — but it's not ready to be the captain. NASA and the European Space Agency use AI to guide rovers on Mars, stop satellites from crashing into each other, and train astronauts. But today's AI is unpredictable and can make mistakes. Anyone who has used ChatGPT knows it sometimes "hallucinates" — that means it makes up wrong information. In space, there's almost no room for error. "If your life depends on it, would you really bank on AI? Probably not," says Sanjoy Paul, a researcher at Rice University. "You still need humans in the loop." Today's AI is good at single tasks. The Perseverance rover uses AI to scan rocks and decide which ones to collect. The Curiosity rover uses AI to zap rocks with lasers. AI can process huge amounts of data faster than humans. But it can't handle unexpected situations like WALL-E does in the movie. Researchers are working on making robots more independent — able to set their own mini-goals. But for now, AI in space is more like J.A.R.V.I.S. from Iron Man: a helpful assistant, not the boss.
why_it_matters: You already use AI in apps, games and homework helpers, so knowing what it is good at — and where it makes things up — helps you decide when to trust it and when to check.

background_read: AI (artificial intelligence) means computer programs that learn from lots of information and then make choices or guesses on their own.
NASA (the United States space agency) landed the Perseverance rover on Mars in 2021, and it uses AI to help pick which rocks to study; the European Space Agency does similar work.
WALL-E is a cartoon movie about a small lonely robot left behind on Earth, and J.A.R.V.I.S. is the clever computer helper in the Iron Man movies.
Rice University (a university in Texas in the United States) is where Sanjoy Paul works, studying how humans and computers can work together safely.
Article_Structure: WHO: NASA, the European Space Agency and researchers such as Sanjoy Paul at Rice University
WHAT: AI already guides Mars rovers, keeps satellites from crashing and trains astronauts, but it still makes mistakes and cannot take charge
WHERE: In space — especially on Mars — and in university labs like Rice University on Earth
WHY: AI is fast at single tasks and huge amounts of data, but space has almost no room for error, so humans stay in the loop

perspectives.description: They point out that AI can sort through huge amounts of data faster than any human, helping rovers choose rocks and stopping satellites from crashing into each other.
Because AI can 'hallucinate' and space has almost no room for error, they say a human should always be ready to step in — you would not bet your life on it.
They are trying to make space robots able to set their own mini-goals, which could help on long missions where astronauts are far from Earth, but they agree the robots are not ready yet.
